ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating and Improving Quality of Emotion Descriptions from Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the quality of emotion descriptions generated by the state-of-the-art audiovisual MLLM, instructor-fine-tuned on the Emotion Recognition In the Wild (EmotiW) challenge dataset, on the Emotion Pesticide dataset, which contains human-annotated, detailed descriptions of emotions in social media posts, spoken word, and user-generated videos. We will use the ROUGE and METEOR metrics to measure the overlap between model-generated and human-written emotion descriptions. We will compare the model with its emotional hallucination-prone variant, and with ablations that remove visual input or emotion-specific tuning data.
CONTROLS: This experiment will serve as a baseline for comparison with future results. 
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved ROUGE and METEOR scores for the model compared with its hallucination-prone variant, but the model's performance might be limited due to its reliance on general emotional cues rather than nuanced human understandings. Additionally, variations in input and data quality could affect the results. 

Paper type and data type were not applicable for this proposal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Spurious Cues and Perception Errors in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the spurious cues and perception errors in the state-of-the-art audiovisual MLLM by applying it to a diverse set of imperfectly-labeled videos from the DVS Emotion dataset with varying levels of emotion intensity, audio quality, and video resolution. We will measure the number and types of spurious cues (e.g., attire color, ambient noise) and perception errors (e.g., associating tears with the sound of crying) in the model's predictions. We will evaluate the model's robustness to different types of perturbations, such as adding or removing visual objects, background noise, and cropping the video frame. We will compare the results with an ablation model with its visual input removed.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with a knowledge-grounded audiovisual memory model, which uses a knowledge graph to guide its reasoning and reduce the influence of spurious cues.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the model to score higher on both spurious cues and perception errors, especially for videos with varying levels of imperfection. We also anticipate that a knowledge-grounded ablation model will outperform the original model in terms of reducing spurious cues and perception errors.

Paper type, data type and experimental domains are applicable for this proposal.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Spurious Cues and Perception Errors in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition
PROPOSAL: We will revise our previous proposal to investigate the regime where the model's hallucinations are more pronounced. We will design a training protocol that encourages the model to make errors, such as removing the reference labels for emotion annotations during part of the training process, to mimic a more challenging real-world scenario. We will apply this protocol to a subset of the DVS Emotion dataset and measure the number and types of spurious cues and perception errors in the model's predictions. We will evaluate the model's robustness to different types of perturbations and compare the results with an ablation model with its visual input removed.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with a model that has been trained on a dataset with augmented labels to encourage it to rely on accurate information.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the model to score higher on both spurious cues and perception errors in this challenging regime, but a knowledge-grounded ablation model will outperform the original model in terms of reducing spurious cues and perception errors.

The previous proposal on Investigating Spurious Cues and Perception Errors in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition is being revised to better align with the results from the first experiment on Evaluating and Improving Quality of Emotion Descriptions.

TITLE: Investigating Spurious Cues and Perception Errors in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition
PROPOSAL: We will revise our previous proposal to characterize the structural inductive bias of the model that leads to spurious cues and perception errors. We will analyze the internal representations and knowledge patterns learned by the model through techniques such as model interpretability, visualization, and diagnostic analysis. We will utilize tools like sensitivity analysis and(destributional robustness based null space projection to identify regions of the input or knowledge space that trigger spurious behavior.

The existing proposal on Investigating Spurious Cues and Perception Errors in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition is being revised to pursue a deeper analysis of the structural bias that contributes to the errors, complementing the experimental approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmenting Audiovisual MLLMs with Multimodal Knowledge Graphs for Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We will augment the state-of-the-art audiovisual MLLM with a multimodal knowledge graph to support more accurate and robust emotion reasoning. We will integrate an emotional event knowledge graph with detailed relationships between emotions, contexts, and cues. We will then fine-tune the augmented model on the Emotion Pesticide dataset and measure its performance on the Emotion Recognition In the Wild (EmotiW) challenge dataset. We will compare the results with the baseline audiovisual MLLM and with a model where the knowledge graph is removed.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with a multimodal knowledge graph trained on a different task, such as image captioning.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the augmented model to significantly improve emotion recognition performance, especially for complex and nuanced emotional scenes. However, its performance might degrade if the knowledge graph contains outdated or inaccurate information.

TITLE: Towards Improving Human-AI Emotion Recognition Workflows with Human Judgment and Alignment
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of human judgment and alignment on the performance and reliability of audiovisual emotion recognition systems. We will collect a dataset of videos with corresponding user-provided emotional annotations, alongside human-annotated explanations for these annotations. We will train a model to predict when human annotators disagree on emotion labels and fine-tune the baseline audiovisual MLLM using these explanations. We will analyze its performance on tasks such as emotion recognition, and emotion-related cue detection.
CONTROLS: We will include a model where a static noisy and another model that was never fine-tuned.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see an improvement in emotion recognition performance for complex emotional scenes, but the model might be sensitive to overfitting due to the relatively small size of our annotation-guided dataset.

The new proposal aims to address open questions related to improving human-AI collaboration and the reliability of emotion recognition systems using human judgment and alignment.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Augmenting Audiovisual MLLMs with Multimodal Knowledge Graphs for Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We will revise our previous proposal to explore the extent to which we can manually curate and validate knowledge graph edges for emotion-related reasoning tasks. We will have human annotators label and validate relationships between concepts in the knowledge graph, such as emotional cues, contexts, and scenes, in addition to pre-training the model on existing multimodal data. We will then assess the fine-tuned model's performance on several emotion-related tasks, including cue detection, and context-aware emotion recognition. We will explore the impact of different curation strategies on model performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with a fully automatic knowledge graph creation approach and another model that was only pre-trained but never fine-tuned.
COST: 35 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant improvement in emotion recognition performance for complex scenes when the knowledge graph is curated with human-validated relationships. However, manual curation might be time-consuming and costly, affecting large-scale deployment.

The revised proposal aims to explore the benefits of manually curating knowledge graph edges for emotion-related reasoning tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Evaluation of Emotion Recognition Datasets and Models
PROPOSAL: We will create a set of adversarial examples for emotion recognition tasks, designed to specifically target spurious cues and perception errors. We will apply these examples to several existing emotion recognition datasets, as well as the models proposed in previous experiments, to evaluate their robustness. We will measure how effectively the models resist confusion when faced with adversarial stimuli. We will investigate whether applying defense mechanisms, such as adversarial training, can improve the robustness of the models.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with a random uniform distribution of data objects.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a range of results, from significant drops in performance to varying degrees of robustness, depending on the models and datasets tested. We anticipate that models that rely heavily on pre-trained language models may be more vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

TITLE: Can Fine-Tuning Avatar-Based Emotion Recognition Models Improve Performance and User Experience?
PROPOSAL: We will explore the possibilities of fine-tuning avatar-based emotion recognition models, designed to interact with users, using multimodal MLLMs that use common MLLM cohosts with a reasonable overlap regarding process patterns. We will compare the results of fine-tuning the models using either human-provided feedback or emulated user interactions. We will evaluate model performance, user experience, and subjective measures of the avatar's emotional intelligence.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with a system that only observes the user's input.
COST: 45 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see an improvement in model performance and user experience, particularly when using fine-tuning with emulated user interactions or real user feedback. However, we anticipate challenges in tuning the avatar's emotional intelligence to align with human expectations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Emotion Reasoning in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition Models
PROPOSAL: Record and release a richly annotated dataset of 10,000 audio-video clips from YouTube videos featuring humans expressing happiness, sadness, anger, and surprise. Clips will be annotated with text descriptions of audiovisual cues that actually contribute to each emotion, as well as data on irrelevant cues that might distract the model. A subset of the dataset will be used to train audiovisual emotion recognition models and measure hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Consists of multimodal contrastive learning (MCL) baselines, as well as data-driven baselines on a controlled audiovisual setting where participants’ facial expressions are matched with unrelated but matched videos of environments to act as control for ablation studies.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to reduce hallucination cases on the dataset by 30%, as models will be specifically trained to ground their predictions on relevant audiovisual cues. However, this result could fail if the high variability in real-world video content limits model generalization.

However, if the manipulations used to generate tests are too artificial, results might not generalize to real-world scenarios.
